title: Airworthiness Directives; Continental Aerospace Technologies GmbH Engines
summary:
The Federal Aviation Administration has issued two new safety orders to prevent engine problems in certain aircraft. One targets a small diesel engine used in light planes; the other addresses unstable thrust behavior on some widebody jets. Both take effect on October 30, with public comments open until December 1.

For the light aircraft engine, the agency is reacting to reports of cracked cylinder heads that can let coolant leak into the engine. Operators must take a one‑time coolant sample and check for contamination. If certain metals or chemicals are too high, the engine’s cooling system must be flushed and refilled, and in the most serious cases the cylinder heads must be replaced. The rule also blocks re‑installing any cylinder head that isn’t considered serviceable. The manufacturer is still investigating the root cause, so this is an interim step and the timeline is short to reduce risk.

For the widebody jets, pilots reported fluctuating thrust during descent when the automatic throttle was in use. To fix this, airlines must update the wiring setup on the flight control computers so a power‑control mode is turned on, helping keep engine power steady and approaches more stable.

Who benefits? Passengers and crews gain from reduced risk of engine overheating, shutdown, or unstable approaches. Maintenance teams and operators get clear, standardized actions to catch corrosion early and head off failures. The orders also align with actions taken in Europe, helping create a consistent global response.

Who might be negatively affected? Owners and airlines face new maintenance tasks, possible downtime, and added costs. The government estimates about $170 per engine for the coolant test, around $360 for a flush and refill, and roughly $11,360 if a cylinder head must be replaced—before considering schedule disruptions. Access to parts and shop capacity could be tight in the near term, and smaller operators may feel the strain more. The agency moved quickly and skipped the usual advance notice due to safety concerns, which may limit early industry feedback, though it is now asking for comments.

Overall, these actions aim to manage immediate risks while longer‑term fixes are developed. Operators will need to plan carefully to meet the deadlines and keep aircraft available, while the broader public should see a net gain in safety.
